content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper considers quantity-enhanced attacks where compromised clients submit large quantities to obtain unfairly high weights in the model aggregation. The authors first compute the $L^1$-distance between each pair of updates and multiply each distance with a quantity-robust distance. Then a group of updates with the smallest quantity-robust
distance to their neighbors are selected. This method is similar to distance-based methods like Krum which assign a score to each client based on pair-wise distances and then select the one with the smallest score. The author further propose a malicious client number estimator, which increases the computational costs of training by running at each iteration.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

I think the strength of this paper is proposing dynamically malicious client number estimator. 

Weaknesses:

The paper is not well-written. I think the proposed FedRA is not robust and it is indeed easy to design a successful attack, which is explained below. The related work is incomplete. There are also serious concerns regarding theoretical results. 

----------

- Based on (4), malicious clients can report very small $q^i$ values and equal but malicious updates (updates in the opposite direction of the average of honest clients) to have the smallest scores and be always selected by FedRA. This way they can move the global model to whatever they want. It seems an attack for FedRA is indeed very straightforward.  


- The considered model includes only one data distribution ${\cal D}$, which does not capture FL in practice where each client has its own unique data distribution. 

- In Assumption 1, it is assumed that for example ${\mathbb{E}}[\partial_k f({\bf w};z)]=\mu_k$ which holds for all $z$. When ${\bf w},z$ are given, $\partial_k f({\bf w};z)$ will not be random any more. So It is unclear what this expectation means. This is the case for variance too. In fact, the authors used such dimension-dependent (and client/example independent) partial gradients in Lemmas 1, 2 which are used for Proposition 1.  

- The structure of the paper should be improved significantly. The authors provided some theoretical results based on a naïve extension of Krum and then introduce their main method in Section 5. I think FedRA including dynamic estimator should be explained right away after describing the model followed by theoretical results.  

- "variance of benign local updates are usually small" The variance can be still quite large depending on the batch-size where it is shown that an adversary can leverage on such variane to design a careful attack (Baruch et al., 2019. Fang et al., 2020, Xie et al., 2020)

Cong Xie, Oluwasanmi Koyejo, and Indranil Gupta. Fall of empires: Breaking byzantinetolerant SGD by inner product manipulation. In Proc. Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence Conference, 2020.

- Several related work have not been cited/compared: 

Dan Alistarh, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, and Jerry Li. Byzantine stochastic gradient descent. In Advances in neural information processing systems (NeurIPS), 2018.

Cong Xie, Oluwasanmi Koyejo, and Indranil Gupta. Fall of empires: Breaking byzantinetolerant SGD by inner product manipulation. In Proc. Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence Conference (UAI), 2020.

Sai Praneeth Karimireddy, Lie He, and Martin Jaggi. Byzantine-robust learning on heterogeneous datasets via bucketing. In International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR), 2022.

Ali Ramezani-Kebrya, Iman Tabrizian, Fartash Faghri, and Petar Popovski. "MixTailor: Mixed Gradient Aggregation for Robust Learning Against Tailored Attacks." Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2022.


- The considered model includes only one data distribution ${\cal D}$, which does not capture FL in practice where each client has its own unique data distribution. 

----------

Minor comment: 

In the definition of $F_i$,  ${\cal D}_i$ should be replaced by $D_i$. 

Partial derivative notation should be defined in Assumption 1 instead of Assumption 2.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a new quantity-aware aggregation rule called QKrum to defend against Byzantine attacks in federated learning. Furthermore, they propose a new federated learning method called FedRA by combining QKrum and a malicious client number estimator. Theoretical analysis and empirical results are both provided in this paper.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: 
1. The idea of using quantity to enhance the defense against Byzantine attacks makes sense. 
2. The performance of FedRA is tested on several datasets.

Weaknesses: 
1. Existing works [1, 2, 3] have emphasized the importance of using history information in Byzantine-robust learning. Furthermore, it has been proved that the optimum cannot be achieved without history information even in strongly-convex cases. 
2. The novelty of this work looks limited. I would appreciate it if the authors explicitly specify the novelty of this work.
3. The readability of this work is not that good. What are the differences between $D_i$ and $\mathcal{D}_i$ (page 3)? Besides, $q^i=||\mathcal{D}_i||$ should be $q^i=|\mathcal{D}_i|$. In Definition 3, $| \nabla h(w)-\nabla h(w')|$ should be $|| \nabla h(w)-\nabla h(w')||$. The authors are suggested to proofread their work.


[1] Allen-Zhu Z, Ebrahimian F, Li J, et al. Byzantine-Resilient Non-Convex Stochastic Gradient Descent[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2012.14368, 2020.
[2] El-Mhamdi E M, Guerraoui R, Rouault S. Distributed Momentum for Byzantine-resilient Learning[J]. arXiv preprint arXiv:2003.00010, 2020.
[3] Karimireddy S P, He L, Jaggi M. Learning from history for byzantine robust optimization[C]//International Conference on Machine Learning. PMLR, 2021: 5311-5319.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The novelty of this work is limited, and the readability also needs to be improved.
content.summary_of_the_review: The idea of using quantity to enhance the robustness of Krum is interesting. However, due to the limited novelty, I think that this work is below the acceptance threshold of ICLR.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper discusses the problem of quantity-enhanced attacks under federated learning setting. Quantity-enhanced attacks will try to degrade the performance of the global model or inject a backdoor by poisoning the local data and submit a large quantity to the central server to amplify the impact of the malicious updates. The authors propose a robust aggregation method called FedRA, which aims to defend against quantity-enhanced attacks and at the same time maintain the performance. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR10, MIND and Adult datasets show that the proposed method outperforms several baseline methods against three poisoning attacks that aim at performance degradation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

- The proposed method performs well empirically compared to other baselines on four datasets.

- Theoretical support is provided to show that the error of FedRA is irrelevant to number of malicious users.

Weakness:

- The paper is poorly written, especially the theory part. Many notations are not clearly defined. To understand the assumptions and propositions, one has to search in the whole paper for the definitions of many notations. For example, Proposition 1 conclusion is that: 
$E(\|g-\mu\|_1)\le \zeta(n,m)\|\sigma\|_1$
However, $g^i$ is defined in the proposition but the definition of $g$ is found in the appendix. In the main paper, the author uses $g^{i*}$. And, what's the take-away from this proposition? Some texts that explain the goal of the proposition will make the paper much clearer, like "it will be used in the proof of Theorem 1". Similarly, for the following theorems and propositions, words are needed to elaborate the goal and logic behind the theory.

- The bad notations and writing style are the key weakness of this paper, making it hard to follow the theory part and proof in this paper.

- Backdoor attack is mentioned in the introduction part but in the experiment part, the method focuses on defending against Byzantine attack (which aims at performance degradation not backdoor injecting). To make it clear, the introduction part should be modified to say that the method focuses on quantity-enhanced Byzantine attack to avoid confusion, or experiments against backdoor attacks in FL should be provided.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:

- As mentioned in the above section, lack of clarity is the key issue of this paper.

Quality:

- It's a good paper with both theoretical support and good empirical results. However, the clarify influences the quality of the paper.

Novelty:

- Security issue of federated learning is an important issue. The method is novel and interesting.

Reproducibility:

- Code and implementation details are provided for reproducing the results.
content.summary_of_the_review: Because of the clarity issue, it's below the acceptance threshold.
